description_full: Pfizer Inc. discovers, develops, manufactures, markets, distributes, and sells biopharmaceutical products in the United States and internationally. It operates in three segments: Biopharma, PC1, and Pfizer Ignite. The company offers internal medicine products, including cardiovascular metabolic diseases products under the Eliquis brand; migraine products under the Nurtec ODT/Vydura and Zavzpret brand; vaccines under the Prevnar family, Abrysvo, Nimenrix, FSME/IMMUN-TicoVac, and Trumenba brands; and Paxlovid for the treatment of COVID-19. It also provides inflammation and immunology products, such as Xeljanz, Enbrel, Cibinqo, Litfulo, Eucrisa, and Velsipity; rare disease products for therapeutic areas comprising amyloidosis, hemophilia, and endocrine diseases under the Vyndaqel family, Genotropin, BeneFIX, Xyntha, Somavert, Ngenla, and Hympavzi brands; and anti-infective and immunoglobulin medicines under the Zavicefta, Octagam, and Panzyga brands. In addition, the company offers oncology products comprising ADCs, small molecules, bispecific, and other immunotherapies for the treatment of cancers, including breast cancer, genitourinary cancer, and hematologic malignancies, as well as melanoma, gastrointestinal, gynecological, and lung cancer under the Ibrance, Xtandi, Padcev, Adcetris, Inlyta, Lorbrena, Bosulif, Tukysa, Braftovi, Mektovi, Orgovyx, Elrexfio, Tivdak, and Talzenna brands. Further, it provides biosimilars under the Inflectra brand; oncology biosimilars comprising Retacrit, Ruxience, Zirabev, Trazimera and Nivestym, and other biosimilars; and sterile injectables, such as Sulperazon, Atgam, Fragmin, Solu Medrol, Solu Cortef, and Bicillin. The company has collaboration agreements with Bristol-Myers Squibb Company; Astellas Pharma US, Inc.; Merck KGaA; and BioNTech SE, as well as a strategic collaboration with Boltz, PBC to develop and deploy biomolecular AI foundation models. Pfizer Inc. was founded in 1849 and is headquartered in New York, New York.

financial_summary: Pfizer, Inc. is a large-cap healthcare business with a $167.5B market cap on $62.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -15% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 5% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $9.1B in free cash flow — roughly 15 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.51× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.9× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 2.8× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 5.8% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 11%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $14.89 to $31.09 (P10-P90).

Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 67% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.4% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The 26 covering analysts target $29.72 on average, 1% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 5% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.63).
It converts 15% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.51x.
ROE of 9% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.4x equity multiplier).
It spends 16.7% of revenue on R&D and 1.3% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.9x net debt to EBITDA ($10.3B of cash against $64.8B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.8x.
Working capital ties up about 192 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -14.6% over 3 years, 8.3% over 5 years and 2.5% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 28%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -5.7% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 0.81 (orders lagging sales), a backlog worth 15% of annual revenue, deferred revenue down 48% and 191 active clinical trials.
Capex runs only 0.4x depreciation (4.2% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 22, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 69%.
Insider trading is two-way: 3 purchases and 1 sale over the past year, net $2.9M bought.
It returns 5.8% a year to shareholders (5.9% in dividends).
It pays out 246% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
